questions.q: A Well-Architected review of a nightly ETL pipeline finds that failed jobs are not retried, there is no dead-letter queue, and reruns create duplicate rows. Which pillar do these findings belong to?

options.why: Wrong: this pillar is about using resources efficiently (right-sizing, partitioning, columnar formats), not recovering from failure.
Wrong: this pillar is about avoiding unnecessary spend, such as lifecycle policies and Spot.
Right: recovering from failure with retries, DLQs and idempotent jobs is the Reliability pillar.
Wrong: this pillar is about reducing environmental impact, such as efficient compute and deleting unused data.

questions.explain: Retries, DLQs and idempotent reruns are failure handling, which maps to Reliability.
questions.remember: Retries, DLQs, idempotent jobs, Multi-AZ, backups and DR → Reliability. Monitoring, alarms, runbooks and IaC for pipelines → Operational Excellence.
variants: The pipeline has no alarms or runbooks → Operational Excellence.
Data is not encrypted with KMS or access is too broad → Security.
Spark clusters are oversized and data is not partitioned → Performance Efficiency.

questions.q: During a Well-Architected review of a data lake, the team discusses S3 lifecycle policies to tier old data and running EMR task nodes on Spot. Which pillar's questions are they answering?

options.why: Right: lifecycle policies, Spot and Savings Plans exist to avoid unnecessary spend.
Wrong: Reliability covers recovery from failure (retries, Multi-AZ, backups), not spend.
Wrong: Security covers IAM, encryption, Lake Formation and audit, not storage tiering for price.
Wrong: this pillar covers running and monitoring systems, IaC and runbooks.

questions.explain: Lifecycle tiering and Spot are cost levers, so they map to Cost Optimization.
questions.remember: Lifecycle policies, Spot, Savings Plans, serverless vs provisioned and less data transfer → Cost Optimization.
variants: The goal is stated as reducing environmental impact (Graviton, deleting unused data) → Sustainability.
The goal is choosing the right engine or file format for query speed → Performance Efficiency.

questions.q: A platform team wants to clean up an old workload in the AWS Well-Architected Tool. A developer in another account it was shared with tries to delete it, and the auditors still want the review history kept. What should the team know?

options.t: Any account the workload is shared with can delete it, and its milestones are kept for audit
options.why: Wrong: only the owner can delete a workload, and deleting removes its milestones.

options.t: Deleting the workload keeps the milestones, which can be restored for 30 days
options.why: Wrong: deleting removes all milestones and cannot be undone.

options.t: Removing the share deletes the workload in the owner's account too
options.why: Wrong: a share only grants access to the workload; it does not control deletion.

options.t: Only the owner can delete it, and deleting also removes all its milestones and cannot be undone
options.why: Right: delete is owner-only and permanent, including every milestone, so keep the workload if the history is needed.

questions.explain: Workload delete is owner-only, removes all milestones and is irreversible.
questions.remember: Only the workload owner can delete it; deleting wipes all its milestones permanently, so keep the workload while review history is needed.
variants: Who is shown as a workload's owner on the Workloads page → its AWS account ID.
Other teams need access to the review → share it with accounts, users, an AWS Organization or OUs.
You want to track progress over time instead of deleting → keep the workload and its milestones.

questions.q: A Well-Architected review flags a high risk issue (HRI) on a reporting pipeline. The business decides not to fix it because the workload is retiring in three months. What is the recommended way to handle this in the tool?

options.t: Mark the best practice as met so the HRI disappears from the improvement plan
options.why: Wrong: a best practice should be marked met only once it is actually fixed.

options.t: Document the reason in the workload notes and record the business approval for not fixing it
options.why: Right: AWS suggests documenting reasons and recording business approval when you choose not to fix a risk.

options.t: Delete the workload and create a new one without that question
options.why: Wrong: deleting is permanent, removes all milestones and hides the risk instead of recording the decision.

options.t: Leave the question unanswered so no risk is shown
options.why: Wrong: unanswered questions hide the decision; the risk is not reviewed or recorded.

questions.explain: Not fixing a risk is allowed, but the reason and the business approval should be recorded.
questions.remember: Risks come from your answers. Fixed → mark the best practice met. Cannot apply it → document the reason in notes. Chose not to fix → record business approval.
variants: The improvement status values to know → None, Not Started, In Progress, Complete, Risk Acknowledged.
The issue would cause a lesser negative impact → it is a medium risk issue (MRI), not an HRI.
Leadership asks for the biggest risks → review the HRIs first.
